excerpt: What a data analyst actually produces, the three tools that cover most of the job, and the questions that separate a report from an answer.

body.text: This lesson explains the data analyst's job: turning a pile of records into an answer somebody can act on. You will learn the three tools that cover most of the work and the questions that decide whether a report is useful.
An analyst does not start with the data. The work starts with a question somebody in the business needs answered by Friday, and the data is the material for the answer.
Before you start

items: About twenty minutes.
A spreadsheet, if you want to follow along by hand.

body.text: The question comes first

items: Ask who will use the answer, and what they will do differently.
Ask what number would change their decision.
Ask by when the answer is needed, since a late answer is usually no answer.
Ask what they already believe, so you can check it.
Write the question in one sentence before opening any file.
If the question cannot be written in a sentence, it is not ready.

body.text: You will see the difference in the first meeting: a vague request produces a forty-page report nobody reads, and a clear question produces one chart and one decision.

body.alt: A spreadsheet with a summary table and a chart beside it.
body.caption: The summary table answers the question. The chart makes the answer visible in five seconds.

body.text: It looks like an analyst spends the day building dashboards. Most of the time goes on cleaning data and asking people what the columns mean.
Three tools, in order of use

items: A spreadsheet, for small tables, quick checks, and charts somebody else can open.
SQL, for pulling records out of a database, which is the most common skill in the job adverts.
A charting tool, for sharing a view that updates without you.
A notebook, if you write code, which suits repeatable analysis.
A shared document, for the answer in words, which is what managers read.
Version notes, so you know which file the answer came from.

body.text: A SQL query will return a table of rows, and reading it is the skill. Learn SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, and JOIN, and you can answer most questions in a small business.

body.alt: A screen showing a SQL query above a table of results.
body.caption: The query is four lines for a simple question. The result table is the material, and the summary is the answer.

body.text: From table to answer

items: Check the row count before trusting a total.
Check for missing values in the column you are summarising.
Check the date range, since a partial month distorts every comparison.
Compare with last period, because a number alone says nothing.
Look for a segment where the pattern is different, which is usually the finding.
Write one sentence: what changed, by how much, and where.

body.text: None of this needs advanced mathematics. Arithmetic, percentages, and care with definitions cover the ordinary work.
Do not worry about the size of the field. Small businesses need this too, and a shop that knows which item sells on Saturdays has an advantage over one that guesses.
Getting the first job

items: Build three small projects with real data you can describe.
One of them should involve cleaning a messy table, since that is the actual work.
Write a short explanation of each project, in plain words, with the chart.
Learn one query language to a working level rather than three to a shallow one.
Look for analyst titles in operations, sales, and finance, not only in technology.
Ask a business you know for one question and answer it for free, as practice.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is a normal mistake, and each is caught by a habit you can build.

items: Your total is wrong: duplicate rows. Count the rows before summing.
The chart says nothing: too many categories. Group the small ones together.
The manager disagrees with the number: agree the definition first, then recount.
The data is missing a month: say so in the report rather than filling it silently.
The analysis takes a week: the question was too broad. Narrow it with the person asking.
Nobody reads the report: lead with the decision, and put the method at the end.

body.text: Practice
Answer one real question with a table you already have.

items: Choose a question from a business you know.
Write it in one sentence, with the decision attached.
Build a summary table with three columns.
Make one chart from the table.
Write the answer in three sentences, and read it aloud.

body.text: You can now see the job behind the numbers. In the next lesson you will take an app idea from a sentence to something on a phone.

excerpt: Turning an app idea into one clear sentence, testing it by hand before writing code, what building actually costs, and how to launch to real users here.

body.text: This lesson takes a mobile app idea from a sentence to something running on a phone. You will write the problem in one sentence, test it by hand, choose a build path, and launch to a small group of real users in Nigeria.
Most app projects fail before any code is written, because the idea is a list of features rather than a problem. One clear sentence fixes that, and it costs nothing.
Before you start

items: A notebook and a pen.
Ten people you can talk to who have the problem.
About an hour for this lesson, and several weeks for the work.

body.text: The first sentence
Write it like this: people who do this, struggle with that, and a simple tool would help them do the other.

items: Name the person, such as a market trader or a lesson teacher.
Name the struggle, in their words rather than yours.
Name the one thing the app would do.
Leave out every other feature, however good.
Read it to three people in that group and watch their faces.
Rewrite the sentence until somebody says they would use it today.

body.text: You will see the sentence get shorter as you rewrite it, and that shortening is progress. An idea that fits in one line can be built, and an idea in five lines cannot.

body.alt: A notebook with an app idea written in a single sentence and a sketch below.
body.caption: One sentence, then a sketch on paper. Paper costs nothing and settles arguments faster than code.

body.text: It looks like the app needs to be built before anybody can judge it. A paper sketch and twenty conversations tell you more in a week than three months of building.
Test it by hand first

items: Write the screens on paper and walk people through them.
Take orders or bookings by hand, using a notebook and your own phone.
Do the job manually for two weeks, and count how often it happens.
Ask what people would pay, and whether they would pay monthly.
Check whether they have data and a smartphone that can run it.
Stop if nobody uses the manual version, since the app will not fix that.

body.text: The manual version will show you the real problems: a name with four spellings, a payment made by transfer, a customer with no email address. Those details decide the design.
You will see a pattern after two weeks: the same three questions, the same two types of buyer. That pattern becomes the app's first screen, and everything else waits.

body.alt: A person testing an app on a phone and writing notes beside it.
body.caption: Testing on a real phone in real light. A design that works on a laptop often fails in a market with one hand free.

body.text: Choose how to build it

items: A no-code tool, which suits a simple form, a list, or a booking, and costs a small monthly fee in dollars.
A cross-platform framework, which builds one app for Android and iPhone from one codebase.
A local developer, who may charge between a few hundred thousand naira and several million, depending on scope.
A partnership, where a developer takes a share rather than a fee, which needs a written agreement.
Website first, if the main job can be done in a browser, which avoids store fees entirely.
Android first, because it covers most of the market here and costs less to test.

body.text: None of these need an office. A single developer working from home is how most Nigerian apps start, and it is cheaper than a team.
Do not worry about the store fees at the start. You can distribute an Android app as a file to your first fifty users, and move to the store when it works.
Launch small, then grow

items: Give it to twenty users who agreed to try it.
Watch three of them use it, without helping, and write down where they hesitate.
Fix the one problem that appears most often.
Add payments only when people ask to pay.
Keep a phone number for support, since trust is built by answering.
Publish on the store once the first fifty users stay.

body.text: If it goes wrong, the first check is whether the problem is real rather than whether the app is good. The sentence at the top of this lesson is the thing to revisit, and most fixes happen there.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is common in a first project, and each has a plain answer.

items: Nobody downloads it: the problem is not painful enough, or the people were never asked.
People download and leave: the first screen asks for too much. Remove a step.
The developer disappears: the agreement had no milestones. Use written stages and a deposit.
The app is too slow on cheap phones: reduce images and test on the cheapest device you can find.
Store review rejects it: read the reason and fix that one item, then resubmit.
Users cannot pay: add a transfer option as well as a card, since cards fail here often.

body.text: Practice
Write the sentence today, and talk to three people this week.

items: Write the problem in one sentence.
Sketch three screens on paper.
Show the sketch to three people in the group you named.
Note the first question each one asks.
Decide whether to continue, based on whether they would use it today.

body.text: You can now take an idea seriously without wasting a year. In the next lesson you will choose where to learn, and how to spot a course that sells nothing.

excerpt: Questions to ask before paying for a bootcamp, night class, or certificate, what an honest provider will show you, and the red flags worth walking away from.

body.text: This lesson helps you choose where to learn: a bootcamp, a night class, an online course, or a certificate. You will ask the questions that reveal whether a provider is real, check the fee against what you get, and walk away from the ones selling hope.
A good provider will answer every question below without hesitation. A provider that dodges two of them is selling something other than teaching.
Before you start

items: The provider's page, open in a browser.
A notebook for the answers.
About twenty minutes.

body.text: Six questions to ask

items: Who teaches, and what is their current job?
What will I have built by the end, and can I see three past projects?
How many hours a week does the course really need?
What happens if I miss a week, or fall behind?
Is the certificate recognised by any employer you can name?
What is the total cost, including registration, exams, and materials?

body.text: You will see the answers either fill a page with detail or stay general. A provider who says the certificate is recognised should be able to name the employer, and most cannot.

body.alt: An evening class with adults at desks and a teacher at a board.
body.caption: A room, a teacher, and a timetable. Ask to visit a session before paying, which most honest providers allow.

body.text: It looks like a certificate is the point of the course. The project you can show is the point, and the certificate only helps if an employer recognises it.
Warning signs

items: A promise of a job or a salary in a fixed number of weeks.
A fee that must be paid in full today, before you visit.
No address, only a phone number and a chat account.
Testimonials with no names, or photographs that look like stock images.
A requirement to recruit other students to keep your place.
Pressure to take a loan through a lender they recommend.

body.text: None of these prove fraud on their own. Two together are enough reason to walk away, and there are always other providers.

body.alt: A laptop showing student project work alongside printed certificates.
body.caption: Ask to see past student work, not only certificates. The work shows what the course actually produced.

body.text: Compare the real cost

items: Add up the fee, the transport, the data, and the hours away from work.
Compare with a free course and a paid mentor once a month.
Check whether the same syllabus is offered free by a recognised institution.
Ask whether the fee can be paid in stages, which most honest providers allow.
Check the refund terms, and get them in writing before paying.
Keep every receipt, in case the course stops halfway.

body.text: A cheaper course that finishes is better value than an expensive one that stops after three weeks. The finishing rate matters more than the fee.
Do not worry about starting later than a friend. A course chosen carefully in three weeks is quicker than a wrong one paid for today.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a route, and the written record is what helps.

items: The course stopped halfway: ask the other students to complain together, in writing.
The teaching is not what was promised: raise it in writing, and request the refund terms.
You paid and heard nothing: report to the platform or the police, with the receipts.
The certificate is not recognised: build a project instead, and show that.
The fee was a loan you cannot repay: speak to the lender early, before the arrears grow.
You chose badly: stop attending and keep the money for the next course, rather than finishing out of pride.

body.text: Practice
Compare two providers using the six questions.

items: Choose two providers for the same subject.
Send both the six questions, in writing.
Note which one answers fully and how quickly.
Ask each for three past student projects.
Decide, and write down the reason for the decision.

body.text: You can now spend on learning without being sold to. In the next lesson you will see the support role that keeps an office working.

excerpt: What IT support actually handles, how to triage a queue by impact, and the habits that make people trust you with their problem.

body.text: This lesson describes IT support work: the queue, the triage, the fixes, and the way a support person talks to somebody whose day has stopped. You will learn how the job is organised and how to start in it.
Support work is mostly diagnosis and communication, not deep engineering. Most tickets are the same twelve problems wearing different clothes.
Before you start

items: About twenty minutes.
Any experience of helping a relative with a phone, which is the same skill.

body.text: The queue, in order

items: Read the ticket and check the impact: one person, a team, or the whole office.
Check who is blocked and for how long.
Start with the problem that stops work for the most people.
Reply once to say you have it, which stops the follow-up calls.
Fix, or find the workaround that keeps them working today.
Close the ticket with what you did, so the next person can repeat it.

body.text: You will see a ticket list with priority labels, and the labels are often wrong. The person who read the impact before the label is the one who gets thanked.

body.alt: A support technician helping a colleague at a desk with a laptop.
body.caption: The fix is half the job. The other half is leaving the person able to work while you finish.

body.text: It looks like support needs to know everything. It needs to find the answer quickly, which is a different and more useful skill.
The twelve problems

items: The password has expired, or the account is locked.
The printer is offline, or the wrong printer is selected.
The network is connected but there is no internet.
The email is full, or the attachment is too large.
A program crashes on opening, usually after an update.
A laptop is slow because of too many startup programs.
A file is missing, and it is in a downloads folder or the recycle bin.
The screen is dark because of the brightness key or a flat battery.
A new device will not join the wifi.
A shared drive is not mapped after a password change.
Sound goes to the wrong output device.
A phone has no storage left.

body.text: None of these need new equipment. A restart, an update, a reconnection, and a cleared cache solve most of them, and knowing that saves an hour per ticket.

When you open a machine, the screen will show the same settings you have seen a hundred times, and the answer is usually in the last place somebody looked. Ask what changed today, because that question narrows the search faster than any tool.

body.alt: An open laptop with a technician checking the inside with a small torch.
body.caption: Hardware is the smaller part of the job. Most days are spent on settings, accounts, and explaining what happened.

body.text: How to talk to somebody whose day has stopped

items: Say what you are going to do, and roughly how long it will take.
Do not blame the user for the fault, even when the cause is clear.
Explain the fix in one sentence, without the jargon.
Ask before taking over their screen, and tell them when you have finished.
If it will take longer, say so before they ask.
Leave them able to do the task, not only with a closed ticket.

body.text: Do not worry about not knowing the answer. Saying you will find out and coming back in twenty minutes builds more trust than a confident guess.
Getting in

items: Learn the basics of Windows or Mac settings, accounts, and networks.
Learn one ticketing tool, since every employer uses one.
Practise explaining a fix to somebody who does not work in technology.
Start with a small office, a cyber cafe, or a school, where the queue is real.
Keep a personal notebook of every problem you solve, which becomes your experience.
Move towards a speciality after a year, such as networks, security, or cloud.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here happens in real offices, and each has a routine answer.

items: You fixed it and it broke again: the cause was not found. Note the pattern and look deeper.
You closed a ticket too early: reopen it, and apologise once rather than twice.
A user is angry: listen to the whole complaint before answering, which usually shortens it.
You broke something while fixing: say so immediately, since a hidden break is worse.
The queue never empties: that is normal. Work by impact, not by arrival order.
You cannot reach a machine: use remote support, or ask the user to read the screen to you.

body.text: Practice
Write three tickets from problems you have already solved.

items: Choose three fixes you have done for family or friends.
Write each as a ticket: symptom, cause, fix, time taken.
Note which one took longest, and why.
Rewrite one explanation so a beginner could follow it.
Keep the three in a notebook as the start of your record.

body.text: You can now see the job that keeps a working day working. In the next lesson you will look at a trade you can start building websites for small businesses.

excerpt: How to sell and build simple websites for local businesses: what to charge in naira, what a client actually needs, and the maintenance that pays monthly.

body.text: This lesson is about building websites for small businesses as a trade. You will learn what a local client actually needs, how to price in naira, what to put in a written agreement, and how maintenance becomes a monthly income.

A small business needs a page that loads fast on a cheap phone, shows what they sell, and gives a phone number that works. That is a smaller job than most beginners imagine, and it is the job people pay for.
Before you start

items: One page you have built yourself, even a simple one.
A way to receive payment, and a written price list.
About an hour for this lesson, and a month to find a first client.

body.text: What the client needs

items: A home page saying what the business does, in one sentence.
Three to six photographs of the work, the shop, or the products.
A phone number and a WhatsApp link, both tappable.
An address or an area, and opening hours.
A short page for prices or services, if the business has them.
A form or a phone number for enquiries, and nothing else.

body.text: You will see that the client's existing page, if they have one, is usually a Facebook page with no address and a blurred photograph. The first job is often to make the phone number findable.

body.alt: A simple business website shown on a phone screen.
body.caption: Test on a cheap phone before showing the client. Most of their customers will see it there, in daylight, on a slow connection.

body.text: It looks like every client wants an online shop. Most need to be found and called, and a shop that does not take payments properly loses more than it earns.
Pricing, in plain figures

items: A one-page site is often quoted between fifty and two hundred thousand naira.
A five-page site with a gallery is often between two hundred and five hundred thousand.
Hosting and a domain usually cost between fifteen and sixty thousand a year.
Charge the domain and hosting separately, so the client sees what renews.
Charge a monthly maintenance fee, often ten to twenty per cent of the build cost per year.
Ask for half before starting and half on delivery, in writing.

body.text: None of these are rules. They are a starting point for a market with a wide range, and a beginner should quote low for the first two clients in exchange for a testimonial.

body.alt: A note showing a domain renewal date beside a laptop.
body.caption: Write the renewal date down and tell the client. A site that disappears on renewal day costs you the client and the reputation.

body.text: The agreement, in one page

items: What is included: the pages, the photographs, and the form.
What is not included: writing all the content, taking photographs, adverts.
The date for the client's content, since delays are the usual cause of late delivery.
The number of revisions, such as two rounds.
Who owns the domain and the hosting account, which should be the client.
What happens on renewal, and what the maintenance fee covers.

body.text: Do not worry about the agreement sounding unfriendly. A one-page summary prevents the argument that ends a good relationship.
Maintenance pays the rent
Ten clients on a small monthly fee is steadier than one large project every quarter.

items: Check the site once a month and confirm it loads.
Renew the domain and hosting before the expiry date, never after.
Update the plug-ins or the software, which prevents most breakages.
Send a short monthly note: visits, enquiries, and one suggestion.
Keep a backup copy of the site and the content.
Charge for changes beyond the agreed scope, politely and in writing.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is common in a small trade, and each has a plain answer.

items: The client does not pay the second half: the site stays on your hosting until payment, which the agreement should state.
The domain was registered in your name: transfer it, since owning a client's name ends the relationship.
The site is hacked: restore from backup, change passwords, and check for old plug-ins.
The client wants endless changes: refer to the revision count in the agreement.
The site is slow: reduce image sizes, which fixes most small business sites.
The client expects customers from day one: explain that the site makes them findable, and adverts bring visitors.

body.text: Practice
Build the first page before you look for the first client.

items: Choose a business you know and sketch one page on paper.
Build it with real photographs and a working phone link.
Test it on a cheap phone on a slow connection.
Write a one-page agreement and a price list.
Show it to the owner and ask for one piece of feedback.

body.text: You can now turn a small skill into a small trade. In the next lesson you will see the work behind a social media account that looks effortless.
